metadata.title: The Artificial Intelligence Crossroads: Build or Buy?
metadata.color_semantics: claude fidelity UI beats at B00/B07/B08/B09. B01-B06 are illustration beats: teal/ink for confirmed facts, crimson/warn for the crack/dip, one terracotta accent per beat per house law.
metadata.greeting_note: HAI word budget: shortest forms only (Hi/Ola/Hej/Ciao). No Wagwan, no in-for-Bear framing — HAI is Bella's own persona, not a stand-in.
metadata.note: Supersedes-in-spirit (does not overwrite) the sibling folder ../the-artificial-intelligence-crossroads, whose fictional 'TechServe/StreamlineOS' scenario is replaced here with a real, primary-sourced case: Klarna's AI customer-service deployment (Feb 2024 launch, May 2025 partial reversal, Nov 2025 hybrid recovery), read through the peer-reviewed Productivity J-Curve mechanism (Brynjolfsson/Rock/Syverson). Thesis: build-vs-buy was never the operative question — Klarna bought (partnered with OpenAI) and still hit the J-Curve dip, because the complementary human-calibration work lagged the rollout. See PEDAGOGY.md for the full evidence table and research prompt trail.

beats.narration_text: Every AI-replaces-jobs headline reads the same on day one — and differently a year later. I pulled one company's actual numbers, what broke, and what they changed. Ciao — HAI here. Here's the pattern that predicts the whole shape of that story before it even happens.

props.segment: The Artificial Intelligence Crossroads: Build or Buy?

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Tanmay Kulkarni. This one's about Klarna's real AI rollout — the launch numbers looked great, then didn't, then came back. I'll walk through what actually happened, and the one framework that explains why it played out that way. Stick around — there's a real lesson here for anyone weighing build versus buy.

props.artifactTitle: The Artificial Intelligence Crossroads: Build or Buy?
artifactLines: The launch looked great — then it didn't.
What changed, and the lesson for build vs. buy.

show.event: three summary lines stagger in top to bottom

beats.narration_text: February 2024: Klarna's AI assistant handles two-point-three million chats in its first month — the workload of seven hundred full-time agents. Sixty-seven percent of all chats. Resolution time down from eleven minutes to under two. On track for forty million dollars in savings. On paper, build-or-buy is already answered.

props.sparkLine: On paper, the answer looks easy.
props.heading: Feb 2024 — 30 days after launch
props.caption: Source: Klarna official press release, 27 Feb 2024

show.event: four stat chips snap in in order

beats.narration_text: But the fine print matters. Analysts point out this was the easiest slice of support work — authenticated users, structured data, common questions. And by May 2025, Klarna's own CEO admits it plainly: 'we focused too much on efficiency and cost. The result was lower quality.'

left.label: What analysts noted
lines: a finite set of common questions

props.caption: Source: CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski, Bloomberg interview, May 2025

show.event: right card (admission) settles in warn red

beats.narration_text: There's a name for this shape: the Productivity J-Curve. Economists Brynjolfsson, Rock, and Syverson showed that a new technology's savings show up before the real work — retraining, redesigning, handling the edge cases — is actually done. The dip isn't AI failing. It's the bill for skipped homework, coming due.

props.dipLabel: the dip: intangible work (retraining, edge cases) not yet done
props.riseLabel: real gains, once the complementary work lands
props.caption: Brynjolfsson, Rock & Syverson — American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics 13(1), 2021

show.event: sparkLine fades in; axes draw on
the J-shaped curve draws left to right
dip label lands as the curve bottoms out, in warn red
rise label lands as the curve climbs, in terracotta

beats.narration_text: So Klarna course-corrected: rehired humans, reportedly for disputes, refunds, hardship cases — the calls that need judgment, not just speed. Routine volume stays with the AI. The complicated cases go back to people.

props.caption: CEO confirmed rehiring (Bloomberg/CNBC, May 2025); task split per industry reporting

beats.narration_text: This is the boundary worth naming plainly: the AI does high-volume, well-defined questions well. Deciding when a case needs a human — a dispute, a hardship, a judgment call — that part doesn't get automated. It's not a bug in the system. It's the design.

show.event: right card (human's job) settles in sage/human tone
brief hold, no caption needed — the line is the point

beats.narration_text: By the third quarter of 2025: the equivalent of eight-hundred-fifty-three agents. Sixty million dollars in annual savings. Response times eighty-two percent faster. A customer satisfaction score of seventy-three. The hybrid model is the one that actually holds.

props.sparkLine: The hybrid model, one year later.
props.heading: Q3 2025 earnings call
props.settleLine: one year later — the hybrid model holds
props.caption: Source: Klarna Q3 2025 earnings call, Nov 2025

show.event: four stat chips snap in in order, terracotta accent

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Build or buy was never really the question — Klarna bought, partnered with OpenAI, and still hit a dip that reads like the Productivity J-Curve: the complementary work lagging the rollout. The real question: are you investing in the calibration work alongside the AI, or skipping it and paying for it later?

artifactLines: Feb 2024: real launch — 700-agent equivalent, 67% of chats, $40M savings on track.
May 2025: real dip — CEO's own words, “lower quality,” humans rehired for hard cases.
Nov 2025: real recovery — 853-agent equivalent, $60M savings, hybrid model holding.
The rule: build-or-buy isn't the question — whether you fund the complementary work is.

show.event: four verdict lines stagger in top to bottom

beats.narration_text: So — build or buy? Klarna bought. And still hit the dip. The J-Curve doesn't check your invoice.

props.sub: ...and still hit the dip. The J-Curve doesn't check your invoice.

beats.narration_text: Your turn — pick a company or industry you're curious about, and run the same check: does the efficiency story and the workforce story actually share one primary source? Read what Claude finds, and see if the J-Curve shows up there too.

cli_exercise.ask: claude "Research how [a company/industry I'm curious about] is deploying AI in a customer-facing role. Find the primary source for their efficiency claims and the primary source for any workforce impact — do the two actually name the same system? Does the company acknowledge a quality dip before improvement, the way Klarna did?"
cli_exercise.output_description: A short sourced brief: the efficiency claim with its source and date, the workforce claim with its source and date, and whether they're actually the same system.
cli_exercise.change: Add: 'Now find one on-record quote from an executive about what they'd do differently.'
cli_exercise.output2_description: The brief gains a fourth line — a direct quote, dated and cited, showing whether the company itself names a dip or a lesson learned.
cli_exercise.next_step: Run it on the next 'AI took the jobs' headline in your own feed.
